title: URL Shortener
brief: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly): given a long URL, return a short link that redirects to it. The interviewer wants a system that survives real traffic, not just a working demo.

rounds.question: Before drawing anything, you get ONE clarifying question. Which matters most?

options.conceptLabel: Should users be able to pick custom aliases?
options.rationale: A real feature question, but it only tweaks the write path's uniqueness check. It doesn't reshape the architecture the way the read:write ratio does — ask it second, not first.

options.conceptLabel: Which cloud provider will we deploy on?
options.rationale: Premature. The design should be provider-agnostic boxes (LB, app tier, KV store, cache); picking a vendor changes none of the reasoning the interviewer wants to see.

options.conceptLabel: What's the total volume and the read:write ratio?
options.rationale: Load shapes everything: 100:1 reads tells you the redirect path is the hot path, which decides where the cache, the replicas, and your attention go. Ask about load before features.

options.conceptLabel: What should the link-creation page look like?
options.rationale: UI is out of scope in a systems interview. Spending your clarifying question here signals you don't know where the hard part of the problem lives.

rounds.question: The redirect endpoint is the hot path. Which API design is right?

options.conceptLabel: GET /{code} responds with an HTTP redirect (302/307) to the long URL
options.rationale: The browser follows a redirect natively — one round trip, no client logic. Using 302/307 (not 301) keeps every click hitting your servers, which preserves the option to count clicks.

options.conceptLabel: POST /redirect with the code in the request body
options.rationale: POST breaks the whole product: a short link must work when pasted in a browser, a chat app, or an email — those can only issue GETs. Semantically it's a read, too.

options.conceptLabel: GET /redirect?code=... returns JSON; the client follows the URL itself
options.rationale: Now every consumer needs custom code to parse JSON and navigate. A bare <a href> or address-bar paste — the main use case — stops working entirely.

options.conceptLabel: A WebSocket channel that streams the destination URL
options.rationale: A persistent bidirectional connection for a single one-shot lookup adds handshake latency and server state for zero benefit. WebSockets are for ongoing streams, not redirects.

rounds.question: How do you generate the short code for each new link?

options.conceptLabel: Hash the URL (e.g. MD5) and take the first 7 characters
options.rationale: Truncated hashes collide — birthday math says you'll see collisions well before exhausting the space, so every write needs a check-and-retry loop. Deduping same URLs sounds nice but most products want distinct links per user anyway.

options.conceptLabel: Base62-encode a unique ID from a counter service — 7 chars covers trillions
options.rationale: Unique IDs can't collide, and base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) packs 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes into 7 characters — decades of headroom at 100M/month. The counter can be sharded (ranges) to avoid a single point.

options.conceptLabel: Expose an auto-increment row ID directly as the code
options.rationale: Sequential decimal IDs are longer (base10 vs base62) and enumerable — competitors can walk /1, /2, /3 and scrape every link you've ever shortened, plus read your growth rate off the counter.

options.conceptLabel: Use a full random UUID as the code
options.rationale: A 36-character code in a product whose entire value is being SHORT. Random 7-char codes could work, but then you're back to collision checks — the encoded counter gives uniqueness for free.

rounds.question: Traffic grows 10x and reads are crushing the store. What's the highest-leverage addition?

options.conceptLabel: Shard the write path across more databases
options.rationale: Writes are 40/s — a rounding error for any store. Sharding the cold path adds operational complexity exactly where the numbers say there's no problem. The reads are the fire.

options.conceptLabel: Move everything to one bigger server
options.rationale: Vertical scaling buys a constant factor, ends at the biggest box money rents, and leaves you with a single point of failure. The interviewer wants to hear a strategy, not a purchase order.

options.conceptLabel: Put a message queue in front of the reads
options.rationale: Queues decouple and absorb WRITE bursts at the cost of latency — the one thing a redirect can't afford. A user clicking a link can't wait for their GET to be dequeued.

options.conceptLabel: Cache hot code-to-URL mappings in memory (and at the CDN edge)
options.rationale: Redirect lookups are immutable and tiny — the perfect cache workload. A small in-memory cache absorbs the popular head of the traffic (links are extremely skewed), and hit rates north of 90% are typical.

rounds.question: Product wants per-click analytics. How do you add them without slowing redirects?

options.conceptLabel: Synchronously increment a counter row on every click
options.rationale: Now every redirect pays a write, and popular links serialize on one hot row — you've put a write bottleneck inside a read path you just spent a round making fast.

options.conceptLabel: Emit an async click event to a queue at redirect time; aggregate out-of-band
options.rationale: Fire-and-forget keeps the hot path at one lookup + one enqueue (microseconds), and the aggregation pipeline can batch, retry, and evolve independently. Losing a rare event under failure is an acceptable trade for redirect speed.

options.conceptLabel: Switch to 301 permanent redirects so browsers cache them
options.rationale: 301 tells the browser to skip your server on repeat visits — great for load, fatal for analytics: the clicks you were asked to count stop arriving at all. This is the classic 301-vs-302 trap.

options.conceptLabel: Have each server log clicks to a local file
options.rationale: Logs scattered across an autoscaling fleet with no aggregation plan aren't analytics — they're an archaeology project. You've deferred the actual problem (collection + aggregation) without solving it.
